result:
The answer 0 is wrong, because the solution's argument only gives a lower bound and cannot show the limit is 0.

The reduction to 3-term-AP-free subsets is correct. So is the observation that each element is the middle of at most one AP triple, which gives at most n−2 triples. The counting argument then yields only h(A) ≳ n^{2/3}. That is a lower bound, and a lower bound of order n^{2/3} cannot show that g(n)/n → 0.

The conclusion is also false. The triples form a 3-uniform hypergraph on n vertices with at most n−2 edges, so the average degree is bounded by 3. A standard Turán-type or greedy independent-set bound for sparse hypergraphs then gives an independent set of size at least cn. Equivalently, h(A) ≥ cn for some constant c > 0. Hence g(n)/n stays bounded away from 0.

I did not derive the exact limit. From memory, the known value is 2/3, though I am not certain of that. In any case it is positive, so 0 is incorrect.

VERDICT: REJECT
